You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),

– likely-relevant recent bug reports,

Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis: 
The test `testStop3()` expects that when parsing the input arguments `--zop==1`, `-abtoast`, `--b=bar` with stopAtNonOption=true, the parser should stop processing further tokens after encountering the first non-recognized long option "--zop==1" and treat the remaining tokens as extra arguments untouched. Thus, the expected extra argument count is 3.

Looking at the main parsing logic in `Parser.parse`, when a token starts with "-", if `stopAtNonOption` is true and the option is unrecognized (`!getOptions().hasOption(t)`), it activates `eatTheRest` and adds that token as an argument. Then it continues to add all remaining tokens as arguments unchanged.

However, the `PosixParser.flatten` method pre-processes tokens before this main parse method. Specifically, it breaks apart tokens starting with "--" and containing "=" by splitting them into two tokens: the option part and the value part. Then, if the token is unrecognized but longer than two characters, it bursts the token into individual option characters plus any remainder. This is done in the `burstToken` method.

The problem is `flatten` ignores `stopAtNonOption` for long options containing '=', because it blindly splits by '=' and adds both parts as separate tokens. Also, it bursts longer tokens not recognized as options, even if stopAtNonOption is true. So these tokens are further split and processed instead of leaving them as-is.

For example, "--zop==1" is split into "--zop" and "=1". "--zop" is unrecognized, but since it contains '=', it has been split incorrectly and the parser sees the parts separately rather than as one unrecognized token and stopping processing. Similarly, tokens like "-abtoast" get burst into "-a", "-b", and "toast" when stopAtNonOption should cause processing to stop and treat the entire token as an argument.

Hence, even though main parse method respects stopAtNonOption after tokenization, the tokenization step itself is aggressive and breaks token boundaries incorrectly, causing the issue described in the bug report and test case failure.

Recent bug reports also indicate that bursting tokens when stopAtNonOption is true is not properly handled, and PosixParser fails to stop processing on unrecognized or non-option tokens as the user expects.

Summary:
- The flatten method splits long tokens containing '=' into multiple tokens even when stopAtNonOption=true.
- It bursts unrecognized tokens into multiple options/arguments even when stopAtNonOption=true.
- This breaks the expected behavior of stopping processing after the first unrecognized option.
- The failing test demonstrates this by asserting there are 3 extra args, whereas the splitting causes this count to be wrong.

The root cause lies in PosixParser.flatten and PosixParser.burstToken where token splitting ignores the stopAtNonOption flag's semantic intent to cease early token splitting and parsing.

Fixing these methods to properly respect stopAtNonOption when encountering unrecognized long options with '=' or during bursting should resolve this failure.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
